name: One-Pot Shrimp & Andouille Jambalaya
description: A bold, soul-warming one-pot jambalaya with plump shrimp and smoky andouille sausage, simmered with the holy trinity, rice, and Cajun spices until every grain is infused with deep Louisiana flavor. Saturday-ambitious but all in one pot.
why: From the family favorites 'want to make' list. Saturday-ambitious one-pot project that fills the house with Cajun aromas. Two proteins (shrimp + sausage) add variety to a week heavy on chicken and pasta.

name: Lamb Kofta Kebabs with Herbed Yogurt & Warm Pita
description: Spiced ground lamb shaped onto skewers and grilled until charred outside and juicy within. Served with a cool mint-dill yogurt sauce, warm pita, and a simple tomato-cucumber side. An irresistible Middle Eastern spread that's great for spring grilling.
why: Satisfies the Middle Eastern requirement. Lamb protein hasn't appeared in weeks. Grilling method fits late-March weather — cherry blossoms and kofta smoke in the air. The yogurt sauce is Elsie's guaranteed dipping win.

name: Korean Gochujang Chicken Lettuce Wraps (Dak-Ssam)
description: Shredded leftover grilled chicken tossed in a sweet-spicy gochujang glaze with quick-pickled cucumbers and pickled daikon, wrapped in crisp butter lettuce cups with steamed rice. Crunchy, saucy, and interactive — kids love building their own.
why: Uses Tuesday's leftover grilled chicken — zero waste, maximum flavor. Korean flavors break up a week heavy on Italian and American comfort. Interactive wraps are perfect for an 8-year-old on spring break.

name: Miso-Glazed Salmon with Sesame Sugar Snap Peas
description: Salmon fillets marinated in sweet white miso and mirin, then broiled until caramelized and flaky. Served alongside crisp sugar snap peas tossed with sesame oil and toasted sesame seeds. A 30-minute weeknight stunner with restaurant polish.
why: Fish protein variety — last fish was branzino 4 weeks ago. Japanese cuisine adds East Asian diversity. Quick broil method makes this a Tuesday-easy dinner despite its stunning caramelized presentation.

name: Chicken Shawarma Lavash Wraps
description: Warm spiced chicken (or leftover grilled chicken re-seasoned with shawarma spices) piled into soft lavash with pickled turnips, garlic toum, fresh herbs, and crunchy vegetables. Wraps travel beautifully — make ahead, eat at room temperature, perfect for flight day.
key_ingredients: chicken thighs or leftover grilled chicken
why: TRAVEL-DAY PICK for Friday. Wraps hold well, eat great at room temperature, and can be assembled in 15 minutes using leftover grilled chicken. Also satisfies Middle Eastern requirement and doubles as a leftover-chicken option.

name: Thai Basil Beef (Pad Kra Pao) with Jasmine Rice & Fried Egg
description: Ground beef stir-fried in a screaming-hot wok with Thai basil, bird's eye chilies, garlic, and a savory fish sauce–oyster sauce glaze. Served over steamed jasmine rice with a crispy fried egg on top. Fifteen minutes from wok to table.
why: Beef protein adds variety. Thai cuisine hasn't appeared in weeks. The ultimate Tuesday-easy dinner — 15 minutes, one wok, explosive flavor. The crispy fried egg on top is Elsie's guaranteed win.

name: Vietnamese Lemongrass Pork Chops with Rice Noodles & Herbs
description: Bone-in pork chops marinated in a fragrant lemongrass-garlic-fish sauce mixture, then grilled until charred and caramelized. Served over cold rice vermicelli with fresh herbs, pickled carrots and daikon, crushed peanuts, and nước chấm dipping sauce.
why: Pork protein we haven't had as chops in any recent week. Vietnamese cuisine adds Southeast Asian diversity. The cold noodle bowl format is perfect for early spring — warming up outside but the cold noodles keep it fresh.

name: Seared Scallops with Spring Pea Purée & Mint Brown Butter
description: Golden-crusted sea scallops perched on a vibrant bright-green spring pea purée, finished with brown butter, fresh mint, and a squeeze of lemon. An elegant 25-minute dinner that celebrates the first flavors of spring in the simplest possible way.
why: Seafood variety different from both salmon and shrimp. French technique with seasonal spring peas — a Saturday-night showstopper that's deceptively simple. Scallops haven't appeared in any recent week. Twenty-five minutes, done.

name: Chimichurri Skirt Steak with Grilled Asparagus & Spring Onions
description: Marinated skirt steak grilled hot and fast, sliced thin against the grain, and drowned in bright, herby chimichurri. Served alongside grilled asparagus spears and charred spring onions for a seasonal South American feast on the grill.
why: Latin American diversity — Argentinian grilling is a world apart from the Mexican tacos of recent weeks. Grilled asparagus celebrates spring produce. Chimichurri is an herbal explosion that Elsie can drizzle (or skip) to taste.

name: Orecchiette with Italian Sausage, Spring Peas & Lemon Ricotta
description: Little ear-shaped pasta tossed with browned Italian sausage, sweet spring peas, a whisper of lemon zest, and generous dollops of creamy ricotta. Light, bright, and distinctly different from the heavier pasta dishes already locked into the week.
why: Satisfies the Italian requirement with a distinctly different pasta personality — orecchiette's cup shape catches peas and ricotta perfectly. Spring peas make it seasonal. Lighter and brighter than Sunday's hearty sausage gravy pasta.

name: Spring Asparagus & Sweet Pea Risotto
description: VEGETARIAN — A creamy Arborio rice risotto studded with tender asparagus tips and sweet spring peas, finished with butter, Parmesan, lemon zest, and fresh chives. The ultimate spring comfort dish that lets peak seasonal produce sing.
why: Vegetarian Italian dinner that's pure spring on a plate. Risotto is a different cooking method (stirred, not baked or boiled) and the asparagus-pea combo is peak East Coast late March. Elsie loves creamy textures and this delivers.

name: Shakshuka with Feta, Spring Herbs & Crusty Bread
description: VEGETARIAN — Eggs gently poached in a spiced, garlicky tomato-pepper sauce, topped with crumbled feta and a shower of fresh dill and cilantro. Served straight from the skillet with thick slices of crusty bread for dipping. A 25-minute one-pan wonder.
why: Vegetarian dinner with North African/Middle Eastern soul. Quick, one-pan, and the dipping-bread format is a guaranteed hit with Elsie. Completely different from anything in the past 4 weeks. No soup — just saucy, spiced comfort.

name: Whipped Feta Dip with Roasted Spring Radishes & Honey
description: Fluffy whipped feta spiked with lemon zest and garlic, spread on a platter and crowned with roasted radishes that turn sweet and mellow in the oven, finished with a drizzle of honey, fresh thyme, and Aleppo pepper. Served with warm pita triangles or crusty bread.
why: Spring radishes are at peak season and roasting transforms their sharp bite into mellow sweetness. A stunning, shareable appetizer that bridges the Mediterranean and Middle Eastern dinners on the menu. Kids love dipping things.

name: Vietnamese Fresh Spring Rolls with Peanut-Hoisin Dipping Sauce
description: Translucent rice paper rolls filled with rice noodles, fresh herbs (mint, cilantro, Thai basil), crisp vegetables, and poached shrimp, served with a creamy peanut-hoisin dipping sauce. Light, fresh, and interactive — let the family roll their own during spring break.
why: Light, fresh contrast to the heartier dinner options. Rolling spring rolls is a perfect spring-break activity with Elsie. Pairs naturally with the Vietnamese pork chops or any Asian-themed dinner night.

name: Spring Niçoise Salad with Seared Tuna, Asparagus & Radishes
description: A composed arrangement of seared rare tuna, blanched asparagus, halved soft-boiled eggs, fingerling potatoes, spring radishes, Niçoise olives, and haricots verts on a bed of butter lettuce — each element placed with intention, not tossed.
dressing: Anchovy-shallot vinaigrette: extra-virgin olive oil, red wine vinegar, Dijon mustard, minced shallot, 2 anchovy fillets (mashed), fresh lemon juice, minced garlic, fresh thyme leaves, flaky sea salt, cracked black pepper
flavor_rationale: The briny anchovy vinaigrette ties together the richness of seared tuna and soft eggs with the bright snap of spring asparagus and peppery radishes. Each composed element offers a different texture — creamy potato, crisp haricots verts, silky tuna — following the French principle of composed contrast where every forkful is a new combination.
seasonal_note: Asparagus and radishes hit peak season on the East Coast in late March through April. Fingerling potatoes are arriving at farmers' markets. This is the definitive spring Niçoise.
why: Composed dinner salad — a complete, elegant meal on a plate. Spring asparagus and radishes replace winter elements for a seasonal update. Substantial enough for a standalone dinner with multiple proteins.

name: Green Goddess Salad with Herbs & Cashew Dressing
description: A crunchy, vibrant tossed salad of finely chopped green cabbage, Persian cucumbers, and scallions drenched in a thick blended green goddess dressing made with fresh basil, spinach, cashews, Parmesan, and lemon. Top with grilled chicken or crispy chickpeas for a full meal.
dressing: Green goddess blender dressing: 1 cup packed fresh basil leaves, 1 cup baby spinach, ¼ cup raw cashews, 2 cloves garlic, 1 small shallot, juice of 2 lemons, ¼ cup extra-virgin olive oil, ⅓ cup finely grated Parmesan, 2 tablespoons rice vinegar, 1 teaspoon kosher salt — blend until thick, smooth, and vibrantly green
flavor_rationale: The dressing is the star — creamy cashews and salty Parmesan provide body and umami, while basil and spinach deliver herbaceous brightness. Lemon and rice vinegar cut through the richness with sharp acidity. Finely chopping all vegetables creates a slaw-like texture that holds the thick dressing in every single crunchy bite.
seasonal_note: Fresh basil and spring herbs are beginning to appear at East Coast markets in late March. The cabbage and cucumber base keeps it crisp and substantial year-round, but the herb-forward dressing shines brightest with just-picked basil.
why: User-requested craving! The modern viral green goddess salad as a tossed dinner — thick herby dressing, maximum crunch. Pairs with any protein from the dinner list or stands alone as a light spring dinner.

name: Shaved Asparagus & Pea Shoot Salad with Lemon-Parmesan Vinaigrette
description: Paper-thin ribbons of raw asparagus and delicate pea shoots tossed with shaved Parmesan, toasted pine nuts, and a bright lemony vinaigrette. An elegant raw preparation that showcases early spring produce at its absolute freshest.
dressing: Lemon-Parmesan vinaigrette: 3 tablespoons fresh lemon juice, 1 teaspoon lemon zest, ¼ cup extra-virgin olive oil, 2 tablespoons finely grated Parmesan, 1 teaspoon Dijon mustard, 1 small clove garlic (minced), ½ teaspoon honey, flaky sea salt, cracked black pepper
flavor_rationale: Raw asparagus is nutty and sweet — nothing like its cooked counterpart. The lemon-Parmesan vinaigrette brings bright acidity and savory umami that amplify asparagus's natural grassy flavor. Pine nuts add buttery richness and pea shoots contribute delicate spring freshness. This is the Italian crudo principle — trusting the raw ingredient to be the star.
seasonal_note: Asparagus is THE marquee spring vegetable on the East Coast, peaking late March through May. Pea shoots are among the very first spring greens at farmers' markets — tender, sweet, and ephemeral.
why: Side salad celebrating peak spring asparagus in its purest raw form. Pairs beautifully with the scallops, risotto, orecchiette, or any Italian dinner. Stunning on the plate with minimal effort.

name: Quick-Pickled Radish & Cucumber Salad with Sesame-Ginger Dressing
description: Thinly sliced spring radishes and Persian cucumbers quick-pickled in rice vinegar, then dressed with a nutty sesame-ginger dressing and topped with toasted sesame seeds and thinly sliced scallions. Bright, crunchy, and palate-cleansing.
dressing: Sesame-ginger dressing: 2 tablespoons toasted sesame oil, 2 tablespoons rice vinegar, 1 tablespoon soy sauce, 1 tablespoon freshly grated ginger, 1 small clove garlic (minced), 1 teaspoon honey, juice of ½ lime, 1 tablespoon toasted white sesame seeds
flavor_rationale: The quick pickle softens the radishes' sharp bite while preserving their crunch. Sesame oil adds warm nuttiness, fresh ginger brings zing, and the rice vinegar–soy sauce combination delivers that addictive sweet-salty-sour balance. This is a palate cleanser — designed to cut through rich mains like jambalaya, kofta, or steak.
seasonal_note: Spring radishes are at their best in late March on the East Coast — sweeter, crisper, and less fiery than midsummer radishes. Their pink-red color against white cucumber makes this salad pop visually.
why: Asian-inspired side salad that naturally pairs with the Korean, Japanese, Thai, and Vietnamese dinners. Spring radishes showcase the season while the quick-pickle method delivers maximum flavor with zero cooking.

name: Albariño (Rías Baixas White Wine)
description: A crisp, aromatic Spanish white wine from Galicia with notes of stone fruit, citrus, and a distinctive saline minerality. Pairs brilliantly with seafood — from the shrimp jambalaya to the miso salmon to the seared scallops. Serve well-chilled at 45°F.
why: A spring-perfect white wine. The saline minerality mirrors the seafood dishes while citrus notes echo the lemon-forward dressings and sauces throughout the menu. Light enough for warming weather, complex enough for Saturday dinner.

name: Hefeweizen (Bavarian Wheat Beer)
description: An unfiltered Bavarian wheat beer with banana and clove notes, refreshingly light body, and hazy golden appearance. Its mild sweetness and lively effervescence make it a natural companion for spiced meats like lamb kofta and chicken shawarma, and it bridges beautifully to Asian flavors.
why: A crowd-pleasing beer that bridges Middle Eastern and Asian flavors — the banana-clove notes complement warm spices like cumin and coriander in the kofta, while the light body refreshes between bites of bold pad kra pao or chimichurri steak.

name: Cucumber-Mint Agua Fresca
description: A refreshing non-alcoholic blend of cucumber, fresh mint, lime juice, and a touch of agave, blended with cold water and strained for a crystal-clear spring drink. Light, hydrating, and universally appealing — including for an 8-year-old who gets to feel like she's having a fancy cocktail.
why: Non-alcoholic option everyone can enjoy, especially Elsie. Cucumber-mint is peak spring refreshment and pairs with everything — the mint bridges to Middle Eastern dishes, the cucumber bridges to Asian options, the lime ties to Latin flavors.
